title: The Aqueduct & The Miradouros
hook: Run the bones of an 18th-century aqueduct, then drop through the city to the river.
story:
Start at the Aqueduto das Águas Livres before the joggers in branded gear show up. The aqueduct ran water into Lisbon for nearly two centuries; the arches that survive march across the valley like a Roman fever dream that wandered too far west.

Follow the spine of the city south. You're losing elevation the whole way, which is the secret to Lisbon — you go down through it, not across it. The miradouros announce themselves: Jardim das Amoreiras, then a sequence of small overlooks where teenagers smoke and grandmothers wait for nothing in particular.

The last kilometer is cobblestones, and cobblestones in Lisbon are not flat. They are an ongoing negotiation with gravity. Slow down. The pastel de nata at the end is going to be too hot to eat anyway.

waypoints.note: Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara

postRunMove: Pastel de nata + bica at Manteigaria. Eat the first one standing at the bar. Order a second.

title: Yanaka at First Light
hook: The pocket of Tokyo the 1923 earthquake and the 1945 firebombs both somehow missed.
story:
Yanaka is the part of Tokyo that doesn't quite know it's Tokyo. The wooden houses lean. The temple bells are real. There is a cat sleeping in front of a noodle shop, and there has been a cat sleeping in front of that exact noodle shop for forty years.

Start at Nippori. The first kilometer is the cemetery, which sounds grim and is in fact lovely: cherry blossoms in spring, cicadas in summer, an unhurried order to the gravestones. Cut west toward Yanaka Ginza, the old shopping street. Run it before the shutters go up. Look at the staircase at the west end — locals call it Yūyake Dandan, the sunset stairs, but at dawn it does the inverse trick.

Loop south through quiet residential streets, past a few small shrines that don't show up on most maps. End in Ueno Park, where the joggers will have appeared, and the day will have officially started without you.
postRunMove: Kayaba Coffee, opened 1938, still serving an egg sandwich that has not been reinvented since.

title: Salisbury Crags & The Volcano
hook: Run up an extinct volcano in the middle of a UNESCO city. Most cities cannot offer you this.
story:
Edinburgh has, by some accident of geology and city planning, an entire wild mountain inside its postcode. Arthur's Seat is 350 million years old and has been extinct since well before the Romans showed up to argue with the Picts.

Start at Holyrood Palace, which the Queen used to live in for one week a year. The Radical Road climbs the spine of Salisbury Crags — it's called Radical because in 1820 unemployed weavers were given the job of building it, which is a very Scottish way to handle unrest. The exposure is real. On a clear day you can see Fife. On a normal day you can see weather coming in.

Loop around the back side, past Dunsapie Loch, then up the summit path. The wind at the top has its own opinions. Coming down, take the long way: the trail south, then back through the meadow where dogs are doing the work dogs were put on earth to do.
postRunMove: Walk five minutes to The Sheep Heid Inn, Scotland's oldest pub. They've been open since 1360. They are not impressed by your run.

title: Sea, Steam, and Sun Voyager
hook: Run between the harbor and a geothermal pool, past a steel ship-skeleton, in the kind of light that doesn't exist anywhere else.
story:
There is a quality to Reykjavík's coastal light that photographers have been failing to describe for a hundred years. It does something to the sea, and the sea does something back. Run this loop and you'll see it three times in different forms.

Start at Harpa, the glass concert hall that looks like a basalt cliff that decided to become architecture. Head east along the seawall. About a kilometer in, you'll pass Sólfar — the Sun Voyager — a stainless steel sculpture that everyone photographs and no one quite understands. It's not a Viking ship. The artist insisted.

Keep going. The path follows the water for several quiet kilometers, past the city's least photogenic stretch, which is when you know you've earned the second half. Loop inland through Laugardalur, where the geothermal pool has been a serious institution since 1908. Finish there. Get in.
postRunMove: Don't shower. Walk straight into the pool. Then a hot dog at Bæjarins Beztu — the one Bill Clinton ate at, which the locals are tired of hearing about and also still kind of proud of.

title: Both Bridges at Dawn
hook: Cross the Brooklyn Bridge before the tourists, return on the Manhattan Bridge while the trains rattle past you.
story:
You have seen the Brooklyn Bridge in approximately four hundred films. None of them have shown you what it's like at 5:50am in May, when the light is doing something unreasonable to the cables and the pedestrian deck belongs almost entirely to runners and one or two cyclists who are technically not supposed to be there.

Start in Brooklyn Bridge Park. Cross into Manhattan over the Brooklyn Bridge — the older one, the prettier one, the one Walt Whitman wrote about and Hart Crane wrote about and a number of people who weren't poets also wrote about. Loop briefly through the financial district, where the cleaners are out and the suits aren't yet.

Return over the Manhattan Bridge. The Manhattan Bridge is the one nobody puts on a postcard, and it is exactly the better run: the subway trains pass at eye level, the view of the Brooklyn Bridge from the Manhattan Bridge is the actual view you want, and the cold steel rattle is the most New York noise there is.
postRunMove: Almondine Bakery, DUMBO. Get the almond croissant. Eat it on the pier, looking at where you just were.
